stories.title: Cloudy skies lead to mixed fortunes for Scotland's eclipse hunters
stories.summary: Scotland's best chance of seeing a solar eclipse in 27 years left some disappointed, though there were moments of magic.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: Cloudy skies lead to mixed fortunes for Scotland's eclipse hunters. Scotland's best chance of seeing a solar eclipse in 27 years left some disappointed, though there were moments of magic. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: Across Scotland, lucky skygazers have caught glimpses of the eclipse - despite cloud covering much of the view.
The Sun disappeared almost entirely behind the Moon, in what was the most dramatic solar eclipse visible from the UK since August 1999.
The spectacle started just after 18:00 on Wednesday evening, and lasted about two hours, with the Sun setting about 21:00.
At the beginning of the eclipse, heavy cloud cover across much of Scotland left visibility poor.
But as the phenomenon progressed, cloud in some areas cleared at least partially, offering glimpses of the rare celestial event.
Parts of Spain and Portugal witnessed the phenomenon of a total eclipse, but in Scotland the eclipse shadow meant that up to 95% of the sun was obscured by the Moon.
At its peak, only an arc of the Sun was visible in Scotland.
In areas where the clouds obscured the view, some viewers reported that it temporarily got a little darker than it otherwise would have been, as the Moon blocked the light from the Sun.
While there will be smaller solar eclipses over the next few years, the next total eclipse will not take place until 23 September 2090.
Experts had suggested that west was best for those hoping to see the eclipse.
They had advised eclipse watchers to find a spot in an elevated location with unobstructed views west.
Whitelee Windfarm at Eaglesham in East Renfrewshire hosted one of the biggest eclipse events in Scotland.

stories.title: Millions in UK and Europe left wowed by once-in-a-generation solar eclipse
stories.summary: More than 95% of the Sun was covered by the Moon in Cornwall, while parts of Spain experienced the magic of a total eclipse.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: Millions in UK and Europe left wowed by once-in-a-generation solar eclipse. More than 95% of the Sun was covered by the Moon in Cornwall, while parts of Spain experienced the magic of a total eclipse. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.
Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.
But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.
Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it serves as a reminder of how "amazing" the universe is.
The path of the total eclipse began at the northern tip of Siberia in Russia, far away from crowds and telescopes.
But it soon began curving around the Arctic Ocean arriving in Iceland in the early evening before sweeping southwards to treat the UK to its wonder.
The partial eclipse began at about 18:00 BST in northern Scotland and just before 18:20 on the south coast of England.
It was imperceivable at first, but for those blessed with cloud-free skies, crowds noticed the Moon nibbling away at the Sun.
Much of central and southern England and Wales enjoyed perfect clear skies giving them an unrivalled view as the Moon moved slowly across the Sun over the course of an hour.
Northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland were cloudier, but it did not stop crowds turning out at famous landmarks across the country.
Some had been successful in acquiring solar eclipse glasses, but the vital eye protectors were in short supply in the run-up to the event with opticians, hardware shops and bakeries all selling out.
But that did not deter people - colanders, cereal boxes and pieces of paper were deployed to offer them a glimpse of the partial eclipse safely.
